summary: In this episode, Fathers Andrew Stephen Damick and Stephen De Young explore the resurrection appearances of Christ, arguing that they are not merely evidence for the resurrection but revelations of Christ's divine identity as Yahweh, the God of Israel, who has come to visit His people. They begin by distinguishing Christ's resurrection (anastasis) from mere resuscitation, linking it to the Old Testament concept of the Day of the Lord, a day of judgment and restoration. They discuss how the Day of the Lord involves the rising of the righteous, the judgment of heavenly and earthly powers, and the establishment of justice. The hosts then examine the resurrection appearances in the Gospels, noting that many people fail to recognize Jesus, which would be poor evidence if the accounts were meant as proof. Instead, they argue these appearances are prophetic visions that reveal Christ's glory and commission the apostles. They also address listener questions about the afterlife, the value of historical-critical scholarship, and the significance of the myrrh-bearing women, St. Peter's restoration, and St. Paul's self-description as 'one born out of due time.' The episode concludes with a call to participate in the resurrection life through the liturgy and to go out into the world as apostles.

entities.title: Jesus Christ
entities.summary: The central figure of the episode, whose resurrection appearances reveal His identity as Yahweh, the God of Israel, and the Lord of glory.

entities.title: St. Paul the Apostle
entities.summary: Apostle who lists resurrection appearances in 1 Corinthians 15, emphasizing their importance as part of the gospel, and who describes himself as 'one born out of due time'.

entities.title: St. Peter
entities.summary: Disciple who denied Christ three times and was restored by Christ in a resurrection appearance, contrasting with Judas.

entities.title: St. James the Just
entities.summary: Brother of the Lord, who received a resurrection appearance and became the first bishop of Jerusalem.

entities.title: Myrrh-bearing Women
entities.summary: Women who first discovered the empty tomb and were the first to see the risen Christ, becoming apostles to the apostles.

entities.title: Lazarus
entities.summary: Raised from the dead by Jesus, serving as a sign that the Day of the Lord has come and that Christ is the Resurrection.

entities.title: Isaiah
entities.summary: Old Testament prophet whose writings describe the Day of the Lord and the judgment of heavenly and earthly powers.

entities.title: St. Mary Magdalene
entities.summary: One of the myrrh-bearers, called the Apostle to the Apostles, who saw the risen Christ and did not recognize Him until He called her name.

concepts.title: Anastasis (Resurrection)
concepts.summary: The Greek word for resurrection, used specifically for Christ's rising, which is not just resuscitation but a cosmic event inaugurating the Day of the Lord and the restoration of all things.

concepts.title: Day of the Lord
concepts.summary: An Old Testament concept of the day when Yahweh visits His people to bring judgment and justice, involving the rising of the righteous and the punishment of the wicked, fulfilled in Christ's crucifixion and resurrection.

concepts.title: Resurrection Appearances
concepts.summary: The post-resurrection appearances of Christ, which are not evidence but revelations of His divine identity, commissioning the apostles and revealing His glory.

concepts.title: Prophetic Vision
concepts.summary: The experience of seeing God, as in the Old Testament, which commissions prophets and apostles; the resurrection appearances are such visions that make the apostles.

concepts.title: Harrowing of Hell
concepts.summary: The Orthodox belief that Christ descended into Hades after His death to liberate the righteous, connected to the resurrection appearances and the Day of the Lord.

claims.text: Christ's resurrection is not a resuscitation to the same kind of life, but a transformation into a new mode of existence, inaugurating the Day of the Lord.
The resurrection appearances are not evidence for the resurrection but revelations of Christ's divine identity, making the apostles prophets.
The Day of the Lord prophesied in the Old Testament is fulfilled in Christ's crucifixion and resurrection, bringing judgment and restoration.
The fact that women were the first witnesses of the resurrection is a deliberate pattern, echoing Old Testament examples where women deliver Israel, and it would not be invented as propaganda.
St. Paul's self-description as 'one born out of due time' is an acceptance of an insult, showing humility and contrasting with his boldness.

The Road to Emmaus, where the disciples do not recognize Jesus until the breaking of bread, illustrating the revelatory nature of the appearances.

The disciples do not recognize Jesus on the shore, yet know it is the Lord, highlighting the mystery of His glorified body.

glossary.definition: Greek for 'resurrection', specifically the rising of Christ, which is not just resuscitation but a cosmic event of judgment and restoration.
